units.Esther 1:1: In the second year of the reign of Artaxerxes the Great, on the first of Nisa, Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, saw a dream.

units.Esther 1:1i: From their cry there came, as though from a small spring, a great river, much water.

units.Esther 4:17k: Queen Esther took refuge in the Lord, gripped by mortal anguish. She took off her glorious garments and put on garments of distress and mourning. Instead of splendid perfumes she filled her head with ashes and dung, greatly humbled her body, and filled every place of her joyful adornment with her tangled hair. She implored the Lord God of Israel and said:
units.Esther 4:17l: “My Lord, our King, Thou art the only one. Help me, who am alone and have no helper except Thee, for my danger is at hand.
units.Esther 4:17m: From my birth I have heard within my ancestral tribe that Thou, Lord, didst take Israel from all the nations and our fathers from all their ancestors as an everlasting inheritance, and do for them everything Thou saidst.
units.Esther 4:17n: Now we have sinned before Thee, and Thou hast handed us over to our enemies because we glorified their gods. Thou art righteous, Lord.
units.Esther 4:17o: Now they are not satisfied with the bitterness of our slavery, but have placed their hands upon the hands of their idols, to abolish the decree of Thy mouth, wipe out Thine inheritance, close the mouth of those who praise Thee, and extinguish the glory of Thy house and Thine altar,

units.Esther 4:17r: Remember, Lord; make Thyself known in the time of our affliction. Give me courage, King of the gods, who dost hold sway over every dominion.

units.Esther 4:17w: Thou knowest my necessity: I abhor the sign of my exalted position upon my head on the days when I appear. I abhor it like a menstrual cloth, and I do not wear it in my days of quiet.
units.Esther 4:17x: Thy slave woman has not eaten at Haman’s table; I have not honored the king’s drinking feast or drunk wine of libations.
units.Esther 4:17y: Thy slave woman has had no joy from the day of my change until now except in Thee, Lord, God of Abraham.
units.Esther 4:17z: God who is mighty over all, hear the voice of those who have lost hope, and rescue us from the hand of evildoers. Rescue me from my fear.”

reread_versions.rationale: Mordecai's dream opens with voices, thunder and an earthquake, before its nations prepare to attack the righteous people. Isaiah joins thunder, earthquake and a great sound in the Lord's visitation, then likens the nations attacking Jerusalem to people dreaming. The shared cluster of tumult, threatened people and dream imagery supports a literary comparison; it does not identify the dream's events with Isaiah's siege or import Isaiah's fire into Esther.

They will be like people drinking and eating in sleep; when they rise, their dream is futile. As a thirsty person dreams of drinking but wakes still thirsty, his soul having hoped in vain, so will be the wealth of all nations who marched against Mount Zion.

reread_versions.relationship: shared imagery of a dark day of distress
reread_versions.rationale: The dream announces a day of darkness and gloom amid the righteous nation's fear of destruction. Joel announces the near day of the Lord as darkness and gloom with turmoil and an approaching force. Both use the same dark-day imagery for overwhelming peril, while Esther's dream and Joel's announcement retain their own settings and are not treated as predictions of one event.

reread_versions.relationship: shared language of darkness and affliction
reread_versions.rationale: Esther's dream calls the coming ordeal a day of darkness, gloom, affliction and distress. Zephaniah similarly accumulates darkness, gloom, affliction and constraint in describing the Lord's day. The dense shared description expresses overwhelming calamity; Zephaniah explicitly names divine wrath against sin, which is not transferred to Esther's threatened righteous nation.

reread_versions.relationship: prayer grounded in remembrance of the Lord's works
reread_versions.rationale: Mordecai implores the Lord while remembering all His works; the following prayer invokes creation and the redemption of Israel from Egypt. The psalm remembers the Lord's works, meditates on all His deeds, and recalls His redemption of the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Both ground an appeal in remembered divine action, without making Mordecai the psalm's speaker or claiming a quotation.

reread_versions.relationship: contrast between mortal royal praise and God's glory
reread_versions.rationale: Esther fears that nations will praise worthless things and admire a king of flesh for ever, in a prayer defending the praise and glory owed to the Lord. Acts depicts a royal audience acclaiming Herod's speech as a god's voice rather than a human being's, followed by his death for failing to give glory to God. The comparison concerns misplaced exaltation of a mortal ruler, not an identification of Herod with Esther's king or of the two occasions.

reread_versions.rationale: Esther asks the Lord to rescue the people and help her, describing herself as alone with no one except Him. The psalmist asks for mercy because he is alone and poor, then seeks rescue from distress and multiplying enemies. Both join confessed isolation to a direct plea for the Lord's protection; the psalm's poverty and requested forgiveness are not added to Esther's words.

reread_versions.relationship: rejection of supposed escape from God's scrutiny
reread_versions.rationale: The royal letter condemns the arrogant supposition that people can escape the justice of God who watches everything. The psalm answers wrongdoers who say that the Lord will not see or understand: the Maker of eyes perceives, disciplines nations and knows human reasoning. Both expose imagined impunity as incompatible with God's perception and judgment, without identifying the psalm's offenders with the letter's subjects.

reread_versions.relationship: rejection of imagined concealment from God
reread_versions.rationale: Esther's letter rejects the thought that the arrogant can evade God's justice while He watches all things. Sirach forbids saying that one will be hidden from the Lord among the multitude and the vast creation, recalls the terror of His visitation, and calls such reasoning foolish. Both challenge presumed escape from divine notice; Sirach's imagined excuse of smallness is distinguished from the letter's arrogance and ingratitude.
